name: Wrist extension hold (isometric)
why: Pushing the back of your hand up against resistance without moving loads the forearm tendon at the outside of the elbow gently. Often eases tennis-elbow pain for a while.
setup: Rest your forearm on a table, palm down, hand over the edge.
Put your other hand on the back of it.
cues: Push the back of your hand up
Your other hand stops it moving
mistakes: Lifting the forearm off the table
feel: Effort along the top of the forearm.
stopIf: Pain above about 3 out of 10 at the elbow.

media.credit: Video: Isometric Wrist Extension for Tennis Elbow (Lateral Epicondylitis) (Momenta Chiropractic)

name: Slow wrist extension with a weight

defaultDose.load: Start light: 0.5-1 kg or a water bottle

why: Slowly lifting and lowering a weight with the wrist strengthens the forearm tendon behind tennis elbow. Tendons get stronger with gradual load.
setup: Rest your forearm on a table or your thigh, palm down, hand over the edge, holding a light weight.
cues: Lift the back of your hand up slowly
feel: Work along the top of the forearm.
stopIf: Elbow pain above about 3-4 out of 10, or worse the next day.

media.credit: Video: Eccentric wrist extension with dumbbell (Physical Therapy First)

name: Grip squeeze
why: Builds grip strength gently. Gripping is what usually hurts with tennis elbow, so it's brought back gradually.
setup: Hold a rolled-up towel or soft ball in your hand, elbow bent and resting at your side.
feel: Work in the hand and forearm.
stopIf: Elbow pain above about 3 out of 10.

media.credit: Video: Towel Squeeze - Ask Doctor Jo (AskDoctorJo)

name: Forearm extensor stretch
why: A gentle stretch for the forearm muscles on the outside of the elbow, nice after desk work or gripping.
setup: Hold your arm out in front, elbow straight, palm down.
cues: Use the other hand to ease it further
feel: A stretch along the top of the forearm.
stopIf: Sharp elbow pain, or tingling in the fingers.

media.credit: Video: Wrist Stretch: Wrist Extensor Stretch for Lateral Epicondylitis (LuWellness)

name: Forearm rotation with a weight

defaultDose.load: A hammer or water bottle held at one end

why: Turning the palm up and down against a light load strengthens the forearm muscles that support the elbow.
setup: Sit with your forearm on a table or your thigh, holding a hammer or bottle upright.
mistakes: Holding the far end of a heavy hammer too soon
stopIf: Elbow pain above about 3 out of 10.

media.credit: Video: Forearm Pronation and Supination With Hammer (OrthoIndy)

name: Wall push-up
why: An easy push-up against a wall builds chest, shoulder and arm strength and is gentle on the wrists.
setup: Stand an arm's length from a wall, hands on it at shoulder height and width.
cues: Bend the elbows to bring your chest in
feel: Work in the chest, shoulders and arms.

media.credit: Video: Physiotherapy exercise: Wall Push Up, for arms, chest and abdominal strength (PhysioMatters Dartmouth)

name: Push-up (knees or toes)
why: Builds upper-body and trunk strength. Start on your knees and move to your toes as you get stronger.
setup: Hands under the shoulders, knees or toes on the floor, body in a straight line.
cues: Straight line from head to knees or heels
Lower your chest towards the floor
feel: Work in the chest, shoulders, arms and trunk.

media.credit: Video: How To Properly Do A Modified Push-Up On Knees - Strength Exercises - Wellen (Wellen)

name: Sit to stand
why: Standing up from a chair without using your hands builds the leg strength that keeps knees comfortable and balance steady. One of the most useful exercises there is.
setup: Sit near the front of a sturdy chair, feet flat and hip-width apart.
cues: Stand up without using your hands
mistakes: Pushing off with the hands (use them only if you need to)
feel: Work in the thighs and buttocks.
stopIf: Knee pain above about 5 out of 10, or dizziness.

media.credit: Video: Chair Exercises Sit to Stand (JW Physio Rehabilitation and Fitness)

name: Heel-to-toe stance
why: Standing with one foot directly in front of the other challenges balance safely: a staple of falls-prevention programmes.
setup: Stand next to a counter or wall.
Put one foot directly in front of the other, heel touching toes.
cues: Touch the counter only if needed
